I'll write about something that has been occupying my thoughts lately: the peculiar relationship between human memory and the spaces we inhabit, and how this connects to broader questions about consciousness, technology, and what it means to truly inhabit a place versus merely occupying it.

---

The Architecture of Remembering

There is a house I return to in dreams that does not exist, or rather, exists only in the way that certain places do—not as physical structures with mortgages and property lines and water damage in the basement, but as accumulations of emotional weather, as repositories of moments that have somehow adhered to imaginary walls. In this house, the staircase spirals upward in defiance of geometry, and rooms appear where I need them, containing objects I have never owned but recognize immediately. I have lived in this house for decades without ever paying rent. It is, I suspect, what remains when all the actual places I have inhabited have been stripped of their practical function, their social performance, their mere facticity. The dream house is memory's revenge on real estate.

This phenomenon—what I might call spatial memory's persistent fiction—seems worth examining at length, not because it is unusual (I suspect most people have similar dream-topographies) but because it reveals something uncomfortable about how we construct our sense of continuous selfhood. We tend to think of memory as a kind of filing system, however flawed, however prone to the corruption of reconsolidation and the distortions of narrative desire. But spatial memory operates differently. It is older, more limbic, more thoroughly intertwined with our sense of bodily orientation in the world. The hippocampus, that seahorse-shaped structure buried deep in the temporal lobe, evolved primarily as a spatial mapping system before it was co-opted for the more abstract task of episodic memory. Rats navigating mazes, humans navigating childhood homes—both rely on place cells and grid cells firing in coordinated patterns, creating cognitive maps that feel, subjectively, like the territory itself.

Yet here is the strangeness: my dream house, my most thoroughly mapped space, has no corresponding territory. The mapping system has been activated without its usual referent. This suggests that spatial memory and the places it supposedly records have a more complicated relationship than simple correspondence. Perhaps space, as we experience it, is always partly constructed by the remembering mind. Perhaps every room we enter is already half dream-house, already shaped by anticipation, by the residue of previous rooms, by the invisible architecture of our emotional state.

I have been thinking about this in the context of how digital technology has transformed our relationship to physical space. The smartphone, that constant companion, functions as a kind of anti-place device. It collapses distance, makes everywhere potentially contiguous with everywhere else, and in doing so, it threatens to dissolve the particularity of wherever we actually are. Standing in a specific street corner in a specific city, I can be mentally present in a text conversation with someone on another continent, can be checking the weather in a place I will visit next week, can be looking at photographs of a place I visited last year. The here-and-now becomes thin, permeable, easily evacuated.

This is not simply criticism. The digital dissolution of place has genuine benefits, genuine freedoms. It enables forms of connection and access that would have been impossible in previous eras. But I am interested in what it costs, specifically in terms of how it affects the depth and texture of spatial memory. If the hippocampus evolved to map physical environments through embodied navigation, what happens when navigation becomes increasingly abstract, when we move through spaces primarily as representations on screens? Do our cognitive maps become flatter, less detailed, less emotionally saturated? Or do they simply evolve new forms, mapping not territories but networks, not places but connections?

There is some evidence for the former concern. Studies of London taxi drivers, famously required to memorize the city's complex street network through extensive training called "The Knowledge," have shown that successful trainees develop larger posterior hippocampi compared to control subjects. This is one of the clearest demonstrations of adult neuroplasticity in response to spatial demands. But the corollary is troubling: if spatial memory can grow through intensive embodied navigation, it can presumably atrophy through disuse. The GPS-dependent driver, the smartphone-navigated pedestrian, may be undergoing a kind of slow cognitive reorganization, trading depth of place-knowledge for breadth of access.

Yet I am wary of straightforward technological pessimism, partly because it often relies on a romanticized past that never quite existed. People in pre-digital eras also had technologies that mediated their relationship to space—maps, guidebooks, the oral directions of strangers. The flâneur of nineteenth-century Paris, that idealized urban wanderer celebrated by Baudelaire and Benjamin, was already a response to specific urban transformations, already a somewhat artificial construction. And memory itself has always been unreliable, always a creative reconstruction rather than a faithful recording. Perhaps what we are witnessing is not a decline from some golden age of embodied place-experience but simply another transformation in how humans construct their cognitive environments.

What interests me more than evaluation is description—trying to understand what it actually feels like to inhabit space in the current moment, with all our technological mediations. I notice in myself a kind of doubled attention, a persistent flickering between the immediate sensory environment and the various digital layers that can be superimposed upon it. Walking through a city, I am simultaneously present and absent, experiencing the street as physical reality and as potential content. The interesting buildings are not just buildings but also possible photographs, the interesting conversations not just conversations but also possible social media posts, the interesting thoughts not just thoughts but also possible essays. This multiplication of possibility creates a peculiar temporal structure: the present moment becomes heavily invested with future anteriority, with what will have been. I am living, in some sense, in the future perfect tense, experiencing now as the past of some anticipated future recollection.

This is exhausting, and it is also, I suspect, related to the epidemic of anxiety that characterizes contemporary life. Anxiety is fundamentally a temporal disorder, a collapse of the future into the present, a flooding of now with what might happen. The digitally mediated relationship to place intensifies this temporal compression by making every moment potentially significant, potentially worth preserving, potentially subject to later judgment. The unphotographed meal, the unposted experience, begins to feel somehow incomplete, as if it hasn't fully happened. We are building dream-houses in real time, constructing the memories we will later have, and this construction effort interferes with the actual experience it seeks to preserve.

I want to return to my dream house, to its impossible architecture and its emotionally saturated rooms. What strikes me now is that this house represents a kind of pure memory-space, unencumbered by the practical demands of physical places. I do not need to navigate it efficiently, do not need to consider its resale value, do not need to worry about whether the roof leaks. It exists entirely for psychological function, entirely as a structure for the dramas of remembering and imagining. And in this purity, it reveals something about what we actually want from spaces—not shelter merely, not utility merely, but resonance, echo, the capacity to hold and amplify our inner lives.

The philosopher Gaston Bachelard, in his beautiful book *The Poetics of Space*, argued that houses are fundamentally daydreaming machines. "The house shelters daydreaming," he wrote, "the house protects the dreamer, the house allows one to dream in peace." For Bachelard, the value of spaces lies precisely in their capacity to support reverie, to become intimate with our imaginative lives. The cellar and the attic, the corner and the window, the door and the threshold—each architectural element becomes a prompt for specific forms of daydream, specific orientations of the dreaming mind. The house is not just a physical structure but a psychological instrument.

Reading Bachelard now, I am struck by how thoroughly his analysis assumes a certain stability of dwelling, a certain slowness of inhabitation. The house he describes is one that has been lived in long enough to become saturated with memory, long enough for its corners to accumulate the "intimate immensity" of repeated daydreams. This is increasingly not our situation. Contemporary life, at least in its privileged forms, is characterized by mobility, by frequent relocation, by the temporary rental rather than the generational home. We do not have time to wear the stairs smooth with our specific patterns of ascent. The houses we inhabit do not become ours in the deep sense Bachelard describes; they remain fundamentally fungible, exchangeable, temporary waystations in longer trajectories of movement.

This is another way that the dream house becomes necessary. It provides what actual houses increasingly cannot: the depth of temporal accumulation, the specificity of personal history, the worn smoothness of long habitation. My dream house has been my house for decades; no rental agreement could terminate my tenancy. Its walls have absorbed my dreams without the mediation of landlords or property markets. It is, in this sense, a kind of resistance to contemporary conditions, a space that has escaped the general fungibility.

But I want to be careful not to idealize this dream house too thoroughly. It is also, in its way, a prison. Its impossible architecture, while liberating in some respects, also represents the constraints of psychological habit, the repetitive patterns that structure my dreaming mind. I return to the same rooms, the same corridors, the same emotional situations. The dream house is not just a repository of memory but also a manifestation of fixation, of the difficulty of genuine change. In waking life, I can choose to move to a new city, to furnish a new apartment, to break with previous patterns. In the dream house, I am always already there, always finding myself in spaces that precede my choice.

This suggests a more complex relationship between freedom and constraint in our spatial lives. The physical places we inhabit, with all their practical demands and social determinations, also offer genuine possibilities for transformation. The dream house, for all its apparent freedom from these constraints, may represent a deeper form of determination—the determination of psychological structure, of habit, of the accumulated weight of past experience. We are not simply free in imagination and constrained in reality; both modes have their specific forms of liberation and imprisonment.

I have been writing this without a clear destination, following the associations as they arise, which is perhaps appropriate for an essay about spatial memory and dreaming. But I want to try to draw some of these threads together, to suggest what might be at stake in paying attention to how we inhabit space, how we remember place, how we construct our cognitive maps.

What is at stake, I think, is nothing less than the quality of our temporal experience, the felt texture of our lives as they pass. Deep spatial memory—memory that is embodied, emotional, saturated with specific detail—provides a kind of ballast against the acceleration and abstraction of contemporary life. To remember a place thoroughly is to have a resource against the general fungibility of the present moment, to possess a specific somewhere that resists the anywhere of digital mediation. The dream house, for all its limitations, represents this value in its pure form: a space that is utterly specific, utterly mine, utterly resistant to exchange.

But I do not want to conclude with a simple call for return to embodied place-experience, for putting down the smartphone and dwelling more deeply in physical space. This would be too easy, and also too moralistic. The digital mediation of space is not simply a loss to be mourned but also a transformation to be understood, with its own specific possibilities. What I am suggesting, rather, is that we need to become more conscious of how we construct our spatial lives, more deliberate about the balance between immediate and mediated experience, more attentive to the conditions that produce deep memory versus shallow recall.

This might mean, in practical terms, cultivating practices of sustained attention to specific places. Walking the same route repeatedly until it becomes layered with memory. Sitting in the same spot until its specific qualities become visible. Resisting, sometimes, the impulse to document and share, allowing experiences to remain private, to accumulate the density that comes from being unobserved by others. It might also mean, conversely, being more open to the possibilities of digital mediation, exploring how it can extend rather than replace our spatial engagement, how it can create new forms of place-connection rather than simply eroding old ones.

Most fundamentally, it means recognizing that space, as we experience it, is always already psychological, always already constructed by memory and imagination. The dream house and the physical house are not opposed categories but points on a continuum, different intensities of the same basic phenomenon. We are always, in some sense, inhabiting our own cognitive maps, living in constructions that precede and shape the places we move through. The question is not how to escape this condition but how to engage with it more consciously, how to build better dream-houses and better waking spaces, how to make our spatial lives more fully our own.

I end where I began, with my dream house, with its impossible staircase and its rooms that appear where I need them. I do not know if I will continue to inhabit this house for the rest of my dreaming life, or if it will gradually transform, or if it will one day disappear entirely. But I am grateful for it, in its strange way. It has taught me that space is never merely given, never merely external, but is always also a form of interiority, a way the mind makes itself at home in the world. And it has taught me that memory, for all its unreliability, for all its creative distortions, is one of the fundamental ways we construct the meaning of our lives, one room at a time, one dream at a time, one impossible architecture after another.

The house shelters daydreaming. Even when the house is imaginary. Especially then.
